title: Design change data capture (CDC)
scopeHtml:
Scope: requirements, API, estimates, log-based capture, snapshots, ordering and delivery, schema evolution, outbox, operations.

Scope: requirements, API, estimates, log-based capture, snapshots, ordering and delivery, schema evolution, outbox, operations.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Change data capture (CDC) turns every insert, update and delete in a database into an ordered stream of events that other systems can consume. Instead of asking the database "what changed?" with repeated queries, you read its own change log. Debezium, AWS DMS, Maxwell, Oracle GoldenGate, Postgres logical decoding and MySQL binlog readers do this. It is the backbone for keeping search indexes, caches, warehouses and microservices in sync.

Functional requirements

  • Capture all row changes (insert, update, delete) from source databases (MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB).
  • Publish them as events (before and after images, operation type, transaction id, timestamp) to a stream.
  • Support an initial snapshot of existing data, then continuous streaming without gaps or duplicates in meaning.
  • Deliver to many consumers: Elasticsearch, Redis, data warehouse, other services.
  • Handle schema changes (add column, rename).

Non-functional requirements

  • Low latency: typically under 1 s from commit to event.
  • Per-row ordering preserved; no change lost; consumers tolerate duplicates (at-least-once).
  • Minimal impact on the source database (a CDC reader must not slow the production primary).
  • Recoverable: restart from the last position without re-snapshotting.

Decision gravity. Choose log-based CDC (read the WAL/binlog) over query-based polling or dual writes. It is the only approach that sees deletes, preserves order, and adds almost no load to the source. Dual writes from the application are the classic trap and are very hard to undo once data has diverged.

Everyday analogy. Instead of repeatedly photographing a notice board to spot changes, you read the clerk's logbook of every change he made.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing "poll with updated_at > last_run": misses deletes and out-of-order commits.
  • Dual-writing to DB and Kafka from app code without a transaction.
  • Forgetting the initial snapshot.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
CDC is mostly infrastructure, but it has two APIs: a control plane (manage connectors) and the event contract consumers see.

Control plane (Kafka Connect REST, as used by Debezium):

POST /connectors
{ "name": "orders-pg",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "database.hostname": "pg-primary.internal", "database.port": "5432",
    "database.user": "cdc_reader", "database.dbname": "shop",
    "plugin.name": "pgoutput", "slot.name": "orders_slot", "publication.name": "orders_pub",
    "table.include.list": "public.orders,public.order_items",
    "topic.prefix": "shop", "snapshot.mode": "initial",
    "tasks.max": "1" } }
201 Created
GET    /connectors/orders-pg/status
POST   /connectors/orders-pg/restart
DELETE /connectors/orders-pg

Property names follow Debezium 2.x; confirm exact keys against the docs of your version.

Event contract (one Kafka message per row change; topic shop.public.orders, key = primary key):

{ "before": { "id": 9001, "status": "PAID" },
  "after":  { "id": 9001, "status": "SHIPPED" },
  "op": "u",                      // c create, u update, d delete, r snapshot read
  "ts_ms": 1731150000123,
  "source": { "db":"shop", "table":"orders", "lsn": 2849201123, "txId": 77123 } }

Consumers read with a consumer group and use source.lsn (or Kafka offset) for ordering and deduplication.

Industry example. LinkedIn built Databus for the same purpose, Netflix built DBLog (and uses it for snapshots without locking), and Debezium (Red Hat) is the common open-source choice. Airbnb's SpinalTap and Uber use similar log readers.

Everyday analogy. The control plane is hiring a court stenographer; the event contract is the format of the transcript pages.

Common interview traps.

  • Message key not set to the primary key (loses per-row ordering across partitions).
  • Treating the event schema as private; it is a public contract that other teams depend on.
  • Omitting the before image so consumers cannot compute deltas.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume an orders database with 5,000 writes/s peak, average row change event 1 KB (with before and after).

Quantity Calculation Result
Event rate 5,000 row changes/s 5,000 events/s
Throughput 5,000 x 1 KB 5 MB/s
Daily 5 MB/s x 86,400 ~430 GB/day (before compression; 3-4x smaller with LZ4/zstd)
Kafka retention 3 days, RF 3 430 GB x 3 x 3 / 3 (compressed) ~1.3 TB
Snapshot 500 GB table, read at 100 MB/s ~85 min
WAL growth if reader stalls 5 MB/s of WAL x 3600 ~18 GB per hour
Consumers 5 groups, each reads full stream 25 MB/s out of Kafka

What this tells you. Throughput is modest, one connector task is enough; Kafka is not the bottleneck. The dangerous number is the WAL growth when the CDC reader is down: the database keeps all logs the reader has not confirmed (a Postgres replication slot pins WAL), and a forgotten slot can fill the primary's disk and take down production.

Everyday analogy. A clerk who refuses to throw away logbook pages until the reader has copied them; if the reader vanishes, the pile blocks the office.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing only Kafka and forgetting source WAL retention.
  • Large multi-GB updates (bulk backfill) creating event storms.
  • Ignoring snapshot duration.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Log reader / connector: connects as a fake replica, reads Postgres WAL via logical replication (pgoutput/wal2json), MySQL binlog (ROW format, binlog_row_image=FULL), MongoDB oplog or change streams; converts to events.
  • Kafka (and Kafka Connect): durable, partitioned, replayable event bus; connector offsets stored in a Connect topic.
  • Schema registry (Avro/Protobuf): versioned schemas with compatibility rules (backward/forward) so consumers survive column changes.
  • Sinks: Kafka Connect sink connectors or custom consumers into Elasticsearch, S3/Iceberg, Redis, other DBs.
  • Monitoring: connector lag, replication slot lag, WAL size, DLQ rate.

Source configuration (Postgres)

# postgresql.conf
wal_level = logical
max_replication_slots = 10
max_wal_senders = 10
max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB     # PG13+: stop the slot from filling the disk (slot invalidated instead)
# MySQL: binlog_format=ROW, binlog_row_image=FULL, server_id=..., gtid_mode=ON

Decision gravity. Read from a replica where the engine allows it (MySQL binlog on a replica is common; Postgres logical slots on standbys arrived in PG16). It protects the primary but adds replica lag and an extra failure point. Reversible, but changing the position source requires care to avoid gaps (use GTIDs). Set max_slot_wal_keep_size so a dead consumer sacrifices CDC, not the primary.

Industry examples. Debezium + Kafka at many companies; Shopify and Zendesk have written about it; Netflix DBLog; Stripe and others mention CDC feeding data warehouses.

Everyday analogy. A news agency (connector) copies every dispatch (change) from a clerk's logbook and teletypes it to many newspapers (consumers).

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving a replication slot orphaned after decommissioning a consumer.
  • Using a statement-based binlog (non-deterministic and unusable by CDC).
  • One giant topic for all tables with no keying.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
How log-based capture works

Every ACID database first writes changes to a sequential log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog/redo, MongoDB oplog) before applying them to data files, so it can recover after a crash and feed replicas. CDC is "a replica that outputs events instead of storing tables".

  • Postgres: wal_level=logical, create a publication (which tables) and a replication slot (a server-side bookmark that guarantees WAL is not deleted until confirmed). The connector streams decoded changes in commit order and sends back confirmed_flush_lsn.
  • MySQL: the connector registers as a replica (needs REPLICATION SLAVE, REPLICATION CLIENT), reads binlog events and tracks file+position or GTID.

Events are emitted at commit, in commit order, with the transaction id, so a consumer can reassemble a transaction. Large transactions (millions of rows) are streamed in chunks in newer versions; confirm behaviour for your version.

Why not the alternatives

Approach Sees deletes Order Load on source Gotcha
Polling updated_at No Weak Heavy queries Misses rows committed late, clock skew
Triggers writing an audit table Yes Yes Adds latency to every write Slows OLTP, schema drift
Dual write (app writes DB and Kafka) Maybe No None Inconsistent when one write fails
Log-based CDC Yes Yes Very low Needs DB config and log access

Decision gravity. Log-based CDC makes the database log (previously an internal detail) a public integration point. The source team must treat log retention and schema as a contract. Hard to retreat from, but the biggest operational win in data integration.

Everyday analogy. A bank keeps a journal of every transaction for audits; CDC just reads that journal.

Common interview traps.

  • Using triggers "because they are easy" and then hitting write latency.
  • Forgetting the replication slot keeps WAL on disk.
  • Believing CDC captures reads.

Initial snapshot without downtime

Problem: the table already holds 500 GB. A consumer needs the full state, then the changes after it, with no gap and no long lock.

Debezium approach: record the current log position (LSN), take a consistent snapshot read (a transaction at repeatable-read isolation), emit rows as op=r, then switch to streaming from the recorded LSN. Short global read lock (MySQL) or none (Postgres exported snapshot).

Netflix DBLog approach: incremental snapshots interleaved with the live stream. Take chunks by primary key range (SELECT ... WHERE id > last ORDER BY id LIMIT 10000), write watermarks to a table before and after each chunk, and drop chunk rows that were also modified in the log between the watermarks. This lets you re-snapshot a single table anytime, pause and resume, without stopping log streaming.

-- Chunk read of the incremental snapshot (PK order, resumable)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 10000;

Decision gravity. Prefer incremental snapshots from day one; the initial blocking snapshot is easy but you will need to re-snapshot (new consumer, bug fix, new table), so the ability to repeat it online is worth the complexity. Reversible.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: new search index has rows that were deleted in the source. Cause: snapshot rows applied after a delete event for the same key arrived. Fix: apply events with a version/LSN comparison (last-write-wins by LSN), and honour tombstones.

Everyday analogy. Photocopying a ledger while clerks keep writing in it; you note the page number at the start so you can add the later entries after.

Common interview traps.

  • Copying the table first, then starting the stream (changes in between are lost).
  • Locking the production table for the snapshot.
  • Not handling deletes that race with snapshot rows.

Ordering, partitioning and delivery guarantees

Key each event by primary key so all changes to a row land in the same Kafka partition and arrive in order. Different rows have no relative order across partitions; for cross-row transaction order, include transaction.id and use the transaction metadata topic, or give the group a single partition per aggregate.

  • Delivery is at-least-once: a connector crash after publishing and before committing its offset replays some events. Consumers must be idempotent: upsert by primary key, ignore events with lower LSN than stored.
  • Kafka Connect exactly-once source support exists in recent versions (KIP-618), but sinks still need idempotent writes; design for duplicates regardless.
  • Tombstones: a delete produces the delete event and a null-value record (for log compaction). Compacted topics (cleanup.policy=compact) can then act as the latest-state table per key and serve as a bootstrap source for new consumers without hitting the database.
-- Idempotent sink upsert guarded by a version
INSERT INTO orders_search (id, status, lsn) VALUES ($1,$2,$3)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET status=EXCLUDED.status, lsn=EXCLUDED.lsn
WHERE orders_search.lsn < EXCLUDED.lsn;

Decision gravity. Partition count and key choice are one-way doors (changing breaks ordering history). Choose the primary key (or aggregate id) as key and size partitions for the future (for example 12 to 48 per busy table).

Everyday analogy. Putting each customer's mail in their own pigeonhole so letters in a pigeonhole stay in the order they came.

Common interview traps.

  • Random partitioning (delete arrives before insert on a consumer).
  • Non-idempotent sinks (duplicate rows or double counted metrics).
  • Assuming total order across tables.

Schema evolution

Add column: new events carry the extra field; old consumers ignore it if the schema is backward compatible. Drop or rename column: breaking. Process:

  1. Register Avro/Protobuf schemas in a registry with compatibility mode (BACKWARD or FULL).
  2. Expand/contract migrations: add new column, dual populate, migrate consumers, drop old after all consumers moved.
  3. Debezium emits the schema change in a separate schema-history topic (needed to decode older log entries, since the log has no column names in some engines such as MySQL binlog).

Never reuse a column name with a new meaning.

Decision gravity. The event schema is an API with unknown clients; treat breaking changes as a versioned new topic (orders.v2) rather than editing in place. Slower, but reversible and safe.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: warehouse loader crashes on a deploy. Metric: DLQ rate and connector task state FAILED. Cause: column type changed from int to string. Fix: compatible change policy enforced in CI against the registry.

Everyday analogy. Changing the form template: older readers must still understand the new forms.

Common interview traps.

  • Renaming a column in place.
  • No registry, JSON with silent field drift.
  • Forgetting the schema history topic.

Outbox pattern: CDC for microservices

Services need to update their DB and publish an event atomically. Dual write fails. Solution: write the business row and an outbox row in the same transaction; CDC reads the outbox table and publishes to Kafka (Debezium has an outbox event router). The event is guaranteed exactly when the transaction commits.

BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=9001;
INSERT INTO outbox(id, aggregate_id, type, payload)
  VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), '9001', 'OrderPaid', '{"orderId":9001}');
COMMIT;

The outbox table grows; delete rows after publishing (CDC reads the log, so deleting the row right away is fine) or partition by day.

Decision gravity. Outbox beats dual writes and distributed transactions for microservice events; the cost is one more table and an extra moving part (CDC). A one-way architectural commitment: all your integrations then depend on CDC health.

Everyday analogy. Writing the outgoing letter and the "to send" slip in one stroke so the postman can never miss it.

Common interview traps.

  • Publishing to Kafka inside the DB transaction callback (not atomic).
  • Using CDC on the business tables and exposing internal shape instead of a clean outbox event.

Operations: lag, failure and cutover

Metrics to watch:

  • Connector lag (source LSN minus confirmed LSN) and MilliSecondsBehindSource.
  • Replication slot retained WAL (pg_replication_slots, restart_lsn vs current).
  • Kafka consumer lag per group.
  • DLQ count and connector state.
-- Postgres: how much WAL is a slot holding back?
SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots;

Failure cases: connector restarts (resume from last offset, duplicates possible); failover of the source (the new primary must have the slot or a GTID continuation; Postgres logical slots are not carried to a promoted standby before PG17, a classic pain, so plan re-snapshot or slot-sync; confirm the version feature); binlog purged before the connector returns (snapshot again).

Cutover to a new pipeline: run old and new in parallel, compare row counts and checksums on a sample, then switch consumers.

Decision gravity. Alert thresholds on retained WAL (for example 10 GB) are cheap insurance against taking down the primary. Reversible and mandatory.

Everyday analogy. Watching how thick the pile of unread logbook pages is getting.

Common interview traps.

  • No alert on slot retention.
  • Assuming failover keeps CDC position automatically.
  • Reprocessing without idempotent consumers.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Why log-based over polling, triggers and dual writes, with their failure modes.
  • Snapshot plus stream consistency and the watermark idea.
  • Ordering by key, at-least-once plus idempotent consumers, tombstones and compaction.
  • Schema evolution with a registry and expand/contract.
  • Source protection: replication slot WAL retention, reading from replicas, limits.
  • Outbox pattern as the microservice answer.
  • Seniors quantify lag, discuss failover of the source, multi-region, GDPR deletes in an immutable log.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing Kafka but not the source-side internals.
  • Claiming exactly-once end to end without idempotent sinks.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• CDC reads the database's own commit log and publishes ordered row-change events; the better alternative to polling, triggers and dual writes.
  • Setup: Debezium connector, Kafka keyed by primary key, schema registry, sinks (search, cache, warehouse).
  • Snapshot then stream without a gap using a recorded log position or incremental watermark chunks.
  • Delivery is at-least-once; make consumers idempotent with versions (LSN) and handle tombstones.
  • Evolve schemas with compatible changes and versioned topics; the event is a public contract.
  • Guard the source: monitor retained WAL, cap slot size, plan for failover; use the outbox pattern for service events.

questions.promptHtml: We need to keep a search index in sync with our orders database. Why not just poll for rows where updated_at is newer than the last run?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic opening test: do you know the failure modes of polling, triggers and dual writes?

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Polling cannot see deletes, misses rows whose transaction committed late (a row with an older updated_at appears after my cursor moved), depends on clocks, and hammers the database with queries. Log-based CDC reads the database's own commit log (WAL or binlog), so it sees every insert, update and delete in commit order with almost no load on the source.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Approach Sees deletes Order Load on source Gotcha
Polling updated_at No Weak Heavy queries Late commits, clock skew
Triggers to audit table Yes Yes Slows every write Schema drift
Dual write Maybe No None Inconsistent if one write fails
Log-based CDC Yes Yes Very low Needs DB config and log access

CDC is "a replica that emits events instead of storing tables". Events carry before and after images, op type, transaction id and log position.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Proposing dual writes from the app without a transaction.
  • Forgetting the initial snapshot.
  • Believing CDC captures reads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does polling ever make sense? -> Tiny tables, no log access, deletes not needed.
  2. Cost of log-based CDC? -> DB config (wal_level=logical, binlog ROW), retained log, connector ops.
  3. Why is dual write worse than it looks? -> A crash between the two writes leaves them divergent forever with no way to detect it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use Debezium". Senior: lists the failure mode of each alternative, and the source-side risk (slot retention).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A updated_at poller silently lost rows from long transactions and nobody noticed until a customer report.

questions.subtopic: Snapshot then stream without a gap
questions.promptHtml: A table already holds 500 GB. How do you give a new consumer the full state and then the live changes with no gaps and no long lock on production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Snapshot and stream consistency is the hardest conceptual part of CDC.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Record the current log position first, take a consistent snapshot read at that position, emit those rows as snapshot events, then start streaming from the recorded position. For re-snapshots without stopping the stream, use incremental snapshots: read primary-key chunks between low and high watermark writes and drop chunk rows that the live log also changed in that window.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Low watermark -> read chunk by PK -> high watermark -> reconcile with log events -> emit

Debezium initial snapshot: remember LSN, repeatable-read transaction, emit op=r rows, switch to the log (MySQL needs a short global read lock; Postgres uses an exported snapshot). Netflix DBLog style chunks keep streaming alive, are pausable and resumable, and work per table.

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 10000;

Consumers must apply events by version (LSN) so a snapshot row arriving after a delete does not resurrect the row.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Copy first, then start the stream (changes in between are lost).
  • Locking the production table.
  • Ignoring deletes racing with snapshot rows.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Time for 500 GB? -> About 85 min at 100 MB/s, throttle to protect the source.
  2. Why prefer incremental snapshots? -> You will need to re-snapshot (new consumer, bug fix) and want it online.
  3. How do you stop deleted rows reappearing? -> Version compare (last write wins by LSN) and honour tombstones.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "dump then replay". Senior: position recorded before the read, watermarks, per-key version guard.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A new search index contained rows already deleted at the source because snapshot rows were applied after the delete event.

questions.contextHtml:
Friday 02:10, the Postgres primary (2 TB disk) pages at 92% disk and rising 18 GB per hour. Query load is normal, autovacuum looks fine, table sizes are unchanged. The Debezium connector task shows FAILED since Thursday 17:00 (a network ACL change). Slot check:

 slot_name   | active | retained
 orders_slot | f      | 410 GB

The checkout service writes 5 MB/s of WAL. A teammate says to run VACUUM FULL on the biggest tables.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: VACUUM FULL (which needs more disk and locks tables) or deleting WAL files by hand, which corrupts the primary.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How long until the disk is full? Do we have another consumer on the slot? Is a re-snapshot acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Time to full: about 160 GB left / 18 GB per hour is under 9 h; act now. Restore connector connectivity if it can catch up fast; if not, drop the slot (pg_drop_replication_slot('orders_slot')), which frees WAL after the next checkpoint, and accept a re-snapshot.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Dead consumer pinning WAL (confirmed by active=f), other WAL consumers (replicas, other slots), long open transactions.
  4. How I'd verify each: SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) FROM pg_replication_slots;, pg_stat_replication, pg_stat_activity for old transactions.
  5. Root cause: The replication slot guarantees WAL is kept until the consumer confirms, so a dead reader grows WAL without bound.
  6. Fix: Short-term: fix network or drop slot, then incremental snapshot to heal. Long-term: max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB (PG13+) so the slot is invalidated instead of the primary dying, with verification of the version behavior.
  7. Prevention: Alert on retained WAL (for example 10 GB), connector state, slot active flag; runbook for decommissioning slots.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sacrificing CDC beats losing production. I would not delete files in pg_wal.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• After the slot is invalidated, consumers? -> Re-snapshot; downstream must be idempotent.
  • Could we have read from a replica? -> Yes on supported versions (logical slots on standbys arrive in PG16), at the cost of replica lag.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A decommissioned consumer left an orphaned slot that filled the primary two weeks later, at the start of a holiday sale.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: VACUUM FULL or deleting WAL.
  • Hire: identifies the slot, drops or fixes it.
  • Strong hire: size cap, alerting, re-snapshot plan, replica option.

questions.contextHtml:
Product reports that cancelled orders still appear in search. A sample row: source DB shows order 9001 deleted. The topic shows events for key 9001: u(status=PAID) lsn=300, u(status=SHIPPED) lsn=310, d lsn=320. The sink code is:

INSERT INTO orders_search (id, status) VALUES ($1,$2)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status;

The connector restarted at 11:02 and replayed about 40 seconds of events. Topic partitions were increased from 12 to 24 last month.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames Kafka for losing the delete event.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the message key the primary key? Does the sink handle tombstones? Did the partition increase change key routing for in-flight data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reconcile the affected ids by comparing search with the source and deleting strays.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Replay delivered old updates after the delete (at-least-once) and the sink applies them blindly, (b) the sink ignores op=d, (c) the partition increase moved key 9001 to a new partition, so old and new events are in different partitions with no relative order.
  4. How I'd verify each: Dump key 9001 from the topic with partition and offset; compare LSNs; look at sink handling of null value records.
  5. Root cause: The sink is not idempotent or version-aware; at-least-once replay plus out-of-order across partitions resurrected state.
  6. Fix: Guard writes with LSN: WHERE orders_search.lsn < EXCLUDED.lsn; keep a tombstone with its LSN for a retention window instead of removing the row, so late updates lose; handle op=d explicitly.
  7. Prevention: Never change partition count on a keyed topic without a planned migration; consumer test that replays events twice and out of order.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not seek exactly-once as the fix; design for duplicates. Soft-deleted tombstones cost a little storage.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compact topic as bootstrap source? -> Yes, cleanup.policy=compact keeps latest per key; delete leaves a tombstone.
  • Total order across tables? -> Not available; use transaction id metadata.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sink that did "delete then insert" on restart replay briefly returned empty results for hot orders; a version guard removed the class of bugs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the broker.
  • Hire: idempotent upsert with a version.
  • Strong hire: partition change effect, tombstone retention, replay tests.

questions.contextHtml: The orders service must update its database and publish OrderPaid for the shipping, email and analytics services. A teammate proposes: commit the DB transaction, then kafka.send() in the next line. Last quarter 0.02% of 3M daily orders (about 600 per day) never produced an event because the pod was killed between the two calls. Another teammate suggests sending to Kafka first, then writing the DB.
questions.promptHtml: Which design do you propose and why? Is it a one-way door?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Retry the send", which does not survive the pod dying.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do consumers need the exact business event or the raw row change? Is the DB Postgres or MySQL (CDC support)? Event ordering per order?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A reconciliation query to find paid orders without shipping events and republish them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Both orderings are dual writes: commit-then-send loses events on crash; send-then-commit emits events for rolled-back transactions.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare counts of paid orders and events per hour.
  5. Root cause: Two systems cannot be updated atomically without a protocol.
  6. Fix: Transactional outbox. In one transaction update orders and insert into outbox(id, aggregate_id, type, payload); a CDC connector (Debezium outbox router) publishes the outbox rows keyed by aggregate_id.
BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=9001;
INSERT INTO outbox(id, aggregate_id, type, payload)
  VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), '9001', 'OrderPaid', '{"orderId":9001}');
COMMIT;
  1. Prevention: Consumers idempotent on event id; delete or partition outbox rows after publishing; alert on connector lag.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: One more table and a dependency on CDC health for every integration: a one-way architectural commitment. I would not use 2PC with Kafka, nor expose raw table rows as the public contract.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Outbox table grows? -> CDC reads the log, so delete rows right after insert or partition by day.
  • Polling publisher instead of CDC? -> Works, higher latency and load; fine at small scale.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After adopting the outbox, the daily missing-event reconciliation went from hundreds of rows to zero, and the same mechanism served three new consumers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retry and hope.
  • Hire: names outbox.
  • Strong hire: both orderings analysed, idempotent consumers, contract vs raw rows.

questions.contextHtml: 10:40 a deploy renames orders.total to orders.total_amount and changes discount from int to string. At 10:41 the warehouse loader task goes FAILED, DLQ rate rises to 2,000/min, search sink keeps working but shows null totals. Connector logs: Schema being registered is incompatible with an earlier schema. Schema registry compatibility mode is NONE. 14 downstream consumers exist, owned by 9 teams.
questions.promptHtml: Stabilise, then design how schema changes should flow.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Rolls back the DB migration under live writes, or edits consumers one by one without a policy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the migration reversible? Which consumers are down and what is their business impact? How far back must DLQ events be replayed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add back a compatible total column populated by trigger or view, restore the old type via a new column, so old consumers resume; pause the loader to stop DLQ growth.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Rename equals drop plus add (breaking), type change breaking, no compatibility enforcement.
  4. How I'd verify each: Registry diff of versions, connector task trace, consumer error logs.
  5. Root cause: The event schema is a public contract but was treated as private table shape, and the registry allowed a breaking change.
  6. Fix: Expand/contract: add total_amount, dual-populate, migrate consumers, drop total after all moved. Set registry compatibility to BACKWARD or FULL and enforce in CI against the registry. Breaking change gets a new versioned topic (orders.v2). Replay DLQ after consumers are fixed.
  7. Prevention: Contract tests, consumer owner list, a schema-change review checklist, schema history topic retained (needed to decode old log entries).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Expand/contract is slower but reversible. I would not rename in place or reuse a name with new meaning.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Json without registry? -> Silent drift; at minimum add a JSON schema check in CI.
  • Old events in the topic after the change? -> Consumers must read both versions (retention window).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single "harmless" rename broke finance reporting for two days because nobody knew the loader existed; an owner registry fixed the discovery problem.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: edits consumers ad hoc.
  • Hire: expand/contract and registry compatibility.
  • Strong hire: versioned topics, CI enforcement, DLQ replay, ownership.

questions.contextHtml: The Postgres primary hardware fails; the standby is promoted in 40 s. Applications recover. But the Debezium connector reports replication slot "orders_slot" does not exist and stops. Slot state was not present on the promoted standby (version predates slot sync, verify for your version). 8 minutes of writes happened on the old primary after the last confirmed LSN; the new primary has a few seconds fewer than the old one. Downstreams: search, cache, warehouse.
questions.promptHtml: Restore CDC correctly and say what you tell downstream owners.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Creates a new slot and resumes streaming, silently losing the window of changes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was failover synchronous (any committed data lost)? What is the last confirmed LSN? Which consumers can tolerate a rebuild?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Create publication and slot on the new primary, note its starting LSN, and mark the gap window as untrusted.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Logical slots are not carried to a promoted standby on older versions; a new slot only sees changes from creation onward.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_replication_slots on the new primary, compare row counts and checksums on sampled keys with downstream.
  5. Root cause: Slot state is local to the old primary and the connector offset points to an LSN of a different timeline.
  6. Fix: Incremental snapshot of affected tables (chunked, online) to heal the gap, with LSN version guards so snapshot rows do not overwrite newer events; long-term, use a version with slot synchronization to standbys or a failover runbook that re-creates the slot and re-snapshots.
  7. Prevention: Quarterly failover drill including CDC, alerts on slot existence, checksum jobs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not claim downstream is consistent without verification; a full re-snapshot costs time and load, incremental costs complexity.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Async replication lost transactions? -> Those commits exist only on the dead primary; business must reconcile.
  • MySQL equivalent? -> GTIDs let the connector resume on the new primary if binlogs are present.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's first real failover revealed that the warehouse held 11 minutes of stale data for three hours because nobody planned the CDC step.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: new slot and move on.
  • Hire: recognises the gap and re-snapshots.
  • Strong hire: online heal with version guards, drills, version caveat marked verify.

questions.contextHtml: Orders DB grows from 5,000 to 50,000 writes/s at peak (a flash-sale season), avg event 1 KB. Today one connector task, topic with 12 partitions, 5 consumer groups. A nightly backfill updates 80M rows. Observations in rehearsal: MilliSecondsBehindSource reaches 90 s at 20k writes/s, Kafka brokers at 25% CPU, connector worker CPU at 100% on one core.
questions.promptHtml: What breaks first and how do you plan for 50k writes/s and the backfill?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more Kafka brokers" (the broker is not the bottleneck).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the backfill necessary on the OLTP table? Is a 10 s lag acceptable at peak? Do consumers need cross-table order?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move backfill to batches with throttling or run it outside the captured tables.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A single connector reads and decodes the log serially, so one task is the limit, (b) event serialization and compression cost, (c) WAL volume pressure on the source, (d) sink consumers too slow.
  4. How I'd verify each: Connector CPU profile, tasks.max and metrics, WAL generation rate, per-group lag.
  5. Root cause: Postgres logical decoding for one slot is single-threaded per slot; throughput of 50 MB/s of decoded events exceeds one reader.
  6. Fix: Numbers: 50,000 x 1 KB = 50 MB/s, about 4.3 TB/day before compression; 5 groups = 250 MB/s out. Split tables across several connectors/slots (hot tables isolated), filter columns with column.exclude.list, compress LZ4/zstd, bump partitions (24 to 48, chosen before data accumulates because changing later breaks ordering), scale consumer groups by lag; backfills in 10k-row batches with sleeps or through a different path marked not captured.
  7. Prevention: Load test at 2x; alert on source-lag and slot size; capacity model per table.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Several slots mean no ordering between tables and more WAL retention risk; partition changes are a one-way door.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Backfill event storm unavoidable? -> Use a flag or separate topic and let consumers skip no-op changes.
  • Multi-region consumers? -> Mirror topics; idempotent consumers regardless.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A nightly 80M-row backfill produced 80 GB of events and held lag at 40 minutes for every consumer; moving it to a throttled batch kept lag under 5 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale Kafka.
  • Hire: splits connectors, partitions, throttles backfill.
  • Strong hire: numbers, slot per hot table trade-off, partition one-way door.
